content: Vancomycin is an antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections, specifically a condition called colitis caused by certain bacteria. This condition often results in diarrhea and abdominal discomfort or pain. Vancomycin is effective only for bacterial infections in the intestines and does not work for bacterial infections in other parts of the body or for viral infections like the common cold or flu. To use this medication, take it orally as directed by your doctor, typically every 6 to 8 hours. The dosage is determined based on your medical condition and response to treatment. If you are also taking bile acid-binding cholesterol medications (e.g. For optimal results, take this antibiotic at evenly spaced intervals and complete the full prescribed course, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Common side effects may include abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting. This medication is prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Serious allergic reactions to vancomycin are rare but possible. If you experience any unusual symptoms, contact your healthcare provider. Before taking vancomycin, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it or have any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. During pregnancy, vancomycin should only be used when clearly necessary, and it is unknown if this form of the medication passes into breast milk. Drug interactions may alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs and herbal products, and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. If someone overdoses and exhibits serious symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately. Otherwise, contact a poison control center. Store this medication in the refrigerator, away from light and moisture. Do not freeze it. Discard any unused medication after 14 days. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. Vancomycin is prescribed only for proven or strongly suspected bacterial infections to prevent the development of drug-resistant bacteria. Severe dermatologic reactions, such as toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP), and linear IgA bullous dermatosis (LABD), have been reported with vancomycin use. If you notice skin rashes, mucosal lesions, or blisters, discontinue therapy immediately and consult your doctor. Vancomycin should be used cautiously in patients with known allergies to corn or corn products, as some formulations may contain dextrose. Rapid intravenous administration may result in flushing, pruritus, hypotension, erythema, or urticaria. Each 100 mL solution of vancomycin injection contains 354 mg of sodium, which may not be suitable for patients with congestive heart failure, elderly patients, or those requiring restricted sodium intake. Prolonged use of vancomycin may lead to fungal or bacterial superinfections. Intracameral or intravitreal administration of vancomycin during or after cataract surgery has been associated with hemorrhagic occlusive retinal vasculitis, including permanent vision loss. The safety and efficacy of vancomycin for these routes have not been established, and it is not indicated for endophthalmitis prophylaxis. Oral vancomycin is indicated only for the treatment of pseudomembranous colitis caused by Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) and enterocolitis caused by Staphylococcus aureus. It is not effective for systemic infections. Clinically significant serum concentrations have been reported in some patients taking multiple oral doses for active C. difficile-associated diarrhea. Vancomycin should be administered intravenously over at least 60 minutes to reduce the risk of infusion-related reactions. Continuous infusion over 24 hours is also an option. Avoid extravasation, as it may cause necrosis. Prolonged use may result in fungal or bacterial superinfections. In pregnant women, available data over several decades of vancomycin use have not identified a drug-associated risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. However, some formulations containing PEG 400 and NADA are not recommended during the first or second trimester due to potential risks observed in animal studies. If vancomycin is required during pregnancy, use formulations free of these excipients. Vancomycin solution has a low pH and may cause chemical or physical instability when mixed with other compounds. Mixtures of vancomycin and beta-lactam antibacterial drugs have been shown to be physically incompatible, with a higher likelihood of precipitation at higher vancomycin concentrations. Adequately flush IV lines between administering these drugs. This medication should be prescribed only for your current condition. Laboratory and medical tests, such as stool samples and kidney function tests, should be conducted while you are taking this medication. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is near the time of the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not double the dose. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about this product. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information tailored to your specific health needs.
